items.title: Final Fantasy Resonance and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 success means "all signals" point to Square Enix making a mainline turn-based JRPG, analyst says: "Just a matter of time"
items.content:
"Square Enix has left a significant chunk of JRPG players behind" by focusing on action RPGs, he suggests

(Image credit: Square Enix) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter As Final Fantasy Resonance has a strong start, and, like Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, proves what an appetite JRPG fans have for turn-based games, one analyst suggests that Square Enix "knows what it's missed out on" after its "move towards more action-oriented Final Fantasy titles."

Square Enix's new turn-based, HD-2D release launched last week and quickly dethroned Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth as the series' single-player games' highest concurrent player peak on Steam. And, as you might expect, that's translated to a lot of money for Square Enix, too.

According to Alinea Analytics analyst Rhys Elliott , Resonance has now sold 400k copies across PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X|S, bringing in $20 million in revenue. That's obviously rather a lot, and Elliott suggests it reflects what JRPG fans actually want and that Square Enix is catering to it. It's also worth keeping in mind that this doesn't include what the game made on the Nintendo Switch 2.

"Given the strong positive reaction to – and early sales of – Resonance and last year's Expedition 33 (which is tracking way better than recent Final Fantasy games), it's clear that Square Enix has left a significant chunk of JRPG players behind during their move towards more action-oriented Final Fantasy titles," he suggests.

"While Square chased more Western trends, a Western company swept in and released Expedition 33, a game JRPG fans wanted for decades and even won game of the year at The Game Awards," he continues. "Square knows this, knows what it's missed out on, and it's seen Capcom succeed on Steam with its legacy franchises where Square Enix has arguably floundered."

Final Fantasy Resonance is the second-biggest Steam launch of any turn-based RPG from Square Enix Final Fantasy Resonance is part of a "resurgence of turn-based RPGs and JRPGs," lead dev says Final Fantasy Resonance dethrones Rebirth for the series' largest Steam peak for a single-player RPG

Obviously, that isn't to say that Final Fantasy Resonance was made in response to Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, as it was in the works well before Sandfall's reveal, let alone its wildly successful launch last year. However, the timing of another turn-based RPG gaining so much traction can't be ignored, and Elliott suggests that Square Enix may consider altering its strategy going forward.

"I can see Square Enix going down a new route, with many diverging paths, for Final Fantasy," he explains. "They've already outlined their plans to go fully multiplatform, smartly moving away from timed PlayStation exclusivity.

"I can also see the company balancing its MMO, high-fidelity remakes, and big-budget mainline Final Fantasy titles with more of these smaller 2D-HD original pixel games alongside the 2D-HD remakes," he continues. "There's still a gap for a turn-based JRPG big-budget Final Fantasy, though, and all the signals are pointing Square Enix in that direction. Just a matter of time, I reckon."

It's not just Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 developer Sandfall that the analyst suggests Square Enix takes notes from, though. After a particularly stellar year with the likes of Resident Evil Requiem, Pragmata, and Onimusha: Way of the Sword – showcasing success with new IP and old favorites alike – Elliott adds: "I'd take even more cues from Capcom, if I were them."

Final Fantasy 14 devs say Evercold's new Evolved mode isn't massive power creep: "If you don't want to change, you don't have to."

items.title: 6 Turn-Based RPGs That Are 10/10 Masterpieces
items.summary: RPGs like Clair Obscur prove that games with turn-based combat still have a place in the modern gaming ecosystem.
items.content:
Maelle looking up at the camera in Clair Obscur Expedition 33 Image via Sandfall Interactive Add CBR on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover By Sage Negron Published Oct 27, 2026, 8:45 PM EDT Sage Negron is a freelance writer based in New York City. He has contributed to CBR in the past, as well as Looper and DualShockers. When he's not writing, he's usually playing video games or reading a good book. Sign in to your CBR account Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Listen Thread 3 Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Turn-based RPGs don't test reflexes and instead require players to rely on careful planning and strategy. While some titles in the genre have fairly simple combat systems, the best RPGs, like Clair Obscur , add new mechanics into the mix that make every battle feel engaging.

While action RPGs have become increasingly common, these RPGs prove there's still plenty of room for turn-based gameplay in today's ecosystem. From JRPGs to titles made in the West, these games prove exactly why turn-based RPGs are so compelling and are must-plays for anyone who enjoys the genre.

Magus Chrono Trigger Boss Battle Image Via Square Enix Few games have aged as well as Chrono Trigger , which is just as enjoyable now as it was when the game was first released back in 1995. While its turn-based combat system may seem fairly standard at first glance, the fact that enemies are visible on screen puts it ahead of games with random encounters from its era.

That said, the best thing about Chrono Trigger is its tech system, which allows two or three characters to team up and unleash powerful Double and Triple Tech attacks. This system naturally encourages players to experiment with different parties and use every character to their fullest.

The battle system in Metaphor: Refantazio is stylistic and dynamic like the Persona games but goes beyond them with its encouragement of making the first blow Image via Atlus Developer Atlus is well known for making exceptional turn-based RPGs, specifically those in the Shin Megami Tensei and Persona series. In 2024, they released an original game in that format titled Metaphor: Refantazio , and it proved that their formula works even outside jof their more popular franchises.

Players take control of a party of magical creatures fighting against a malevolent prince trying to usurp the throne of the fantasy land of Euchronia and spread darkness across the land. Like similar Atlus games, gameplay is divided between battling monsters in dungeons and spending time with party members to increase stats. Both are layered under a fantastic story filled with unexpected twists and over-the-top boss battles.

The game proudly embraces many of the fantasy genre tropes, while also offering a unique spin on the genre that only Atlus can pull off. Metaphor: Refantazio could be the start of a great franchise that continues on for years, or an amazing one-off experience that stands on its own. Either way, it’s still a fantastic game .

Image via Intelligent Systems The Fire Emblem franchise is one of the premier strategy RPGs currently on the market. Ever since Fire Emblem Awakening reinvigorated the franchise on the Nintendo 3DS, the series has enjoyed plenty of mainstream success. The first mainline entry for the Nintendo Switch, Fire Emblem: Three Houses , was another fine entry.

As a professor at a prestigious military school, there are three different students that players can take under their wing. This can lead to several different outcomes requiring multiple playthroughs to get the full experience. Each of these paths allows players to command different battalions in tactical turn-based combat.

All franchises have things that don't make sense, and the Fire Emblem has no shortage of head-scratching details.

items.title: 10 Turn-Based RPGs With Virtually Perfect Combat Systems
items.summary: RPGs like Fire Emblem and Baldur's Gate have helped to refine turn-based combat to perfection.
items.content:
Gustave, Maelle, Lune, and Sciel exploring on the island in the early parts of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Image via Sandfall Interactive Add CBR on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover By Sage Negron Published Oct 24, 2026, 1:15 PM EDT Sage Negron is a freelance writer based in New York City. He has contributed to CBR in the past, as well as Looper and DualShockers. When he's not writing, he's usually playing video games or reading a good book. Sign in to your CBR account Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Listen Thread 2 Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Making a great combat system in a turn-based RPG is not easy. After all, there are so many games that feature this kind of system that each new one has to find a way to innovate in order for it to stand out.

Luckily, there are plenty of fantastic turn-based RPGs that put their own spin on the genre. And many of them also have strong stories and exceptional party members to match their great gameplay.

The protagonist's All Out Attack portrait, raising a hand to adjust his collar, from Persona 3 Reload. Image via Atlus Persona 3 Reload remade the PS2 classic from the ground up with many of the quality of life changes that made Persona 5 Royal such a smash. The turn-based combat also received some smart new additions to make battling more fun.

The player now has more control over party members, the Shift mechanic helps players take advantage of hitting enemy weaknesses, and the Theurgy moves add even more cinematic flair to finishing off battles. Persona 3 Reload ’s combat is easily the best in the series.

Baldur's Gate 3 Combat Image via Larian Studios Turn-based battles are just one of the many amazing aspects of Baldur’s Gate 3 . With just one roll of the d20 dice, a wide array of combat options are triggered that make each battle feel different from the last.

From there, it becomes an entirely new game, managing stats, using different magic attacks, and trying to get the advantage over enemies. Those experienced with tabletop RPGs will feel right at home with Baldur’s Gate 3 .

4 graded cards, 6 seconds each. Faster answers score more.

Must be 18+/19+ to participate depending on jurisdiction.

Clair Obscur Expedition 33 battle system Image via Sandfall Games Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 combined a lot of different systems to create engaging turn-based combat. Players have to juggle elemental affinities, action commands, and powerful special attacks each time they get into battle.

In addition, stat boosts from Pictos and Luminas can change how each battle goes. Parrying attacks can save a player’s life, and stunning an opponent at the right time is crucial.

The pyrokinetic ability Ignition in Divinity: Original Sin II. Image via Larian Studios Tactical strategy games offer some of the best turn-based combat around. Divinity: Original Sin II , from the makers of Baldur’s Gate 3 , offers a flexible combat system that adapts to whatever party that the player builds.

Players can take advantage of both the environment and the elements, break an opponent’s armor, and take the high ground to make the best use of the open-ended class system. Divinity: Original Sin II has a little bit of everything for everyone.

Octopath Traveler Screenshot of a character fighting enemes in turn based combat Image via Square Enix There are eight characters that the player can choose to follow the story of in Octopath Traveler . No matter what path the player takes, the turn-based combat remains just as fulfilling.

Combat revolves around the Break and Boost system. Destroying an opponent’s guard will Break them and leave them defenseless, and Boost points are used to inflict even more damage.

items.title: Expedition 33's Fan-favorite Costumes Are Unofficially Invading a Different Game
items.summary: Every game needs a baguette outfit
items.content:
Listen Thread Link copied to clipboard By Austin Manchester Published Oct 21, 2026, 12:01 PM EDT Austin Manchester is a writer and editor living in New York City. At Polygon, he covers gaming and entertainment news, reviews new video games, interviews behind-the-scenes talent, and more. He enjoys discovering hidden gems and sharing them with Polygon's audience. Previously, he was the gaming editor for AIPT Comics and has written for other outlets like XDA, How-To Geek, and The List. He enjoys soulslikes, character-driven RPGs, and third-person shooters plucked straight out of the Xbox 360 era. He also likes to flex his non-video game nerdy knowledge sometimes, whether that's explaining who's who in the new Wolverine game or recommending a comic book series about a sentient sword. News Every game needs a baguette outfit

Image: Sandfall Interactive/Kepler Interactive Add Polygon.com on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover Rayman Legends Retold Sign in to your Polygon.com account Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Listen Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Sandfall Interactive's award-winning Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 took the gaming world by storm last year as players enjoyed the role-playing game's serious themes and its goofy bits , like the "baguette" outfits. Equip those, and the downtrodden expeditioners will suddenly look as silly as can be with red berets, black-and-white-striped shirts, and baguettes tied to their backs.

In just a few weeks, those beloved baguette outfits will unofficially make their way into a new game from a different French studio as a way of paying homage to Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 .

Close Image: Ubisoft Image: Ubisoft Image: Ubisoft window.arrayOfGalleries["article-gallery-1-256138651"] = '" Close Image: Ubisoft Image: Ubisoft Image: Ubisoft "'; In December's Rayman Legends Retold , Rayman and Barbara will get their own baguette outfits. While the news release doesn't explicitly state they're inspired by Expedition 33 , it does say the outfits "offer a playful nod to a fellow game created in Montpellier." So, you know. Expedition 33 . "Subtly, [the outfits] honor a title that holds a special place in the hearts of the development team," the news release states, making me think Ubisoft and I have different definitions of the word "subtly."

The original Rayman Legends came out in 2013, so it's not quite as old as o ther games that are getting remakes this year. Ubisoft decided to remake Rayman's most recent game as a way to introduce the franchise to a new audience because "it's the richest version of the world, the widest set of characters," brand manager Loïc Gounon told Polygon .

From what we've played so far, Ubisoft is succeeding. " Rayman Legends Retold is an imaginative platformer offering vibrant worlds, engaging platforming sequences, and endearing personality that oozes from every beautiful crack in its wacky world," Polygon's Jason Venter wrote in his preview of the upcoming game .

Rayman Legends Retold will be released on Dec. 3 for Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X. The baguette outfits will be available at launch, and you won't have to unlock or purchase them.

items.title: Game Pass Is About To Lose Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 And Some Other Incredible Games
items.summary: The RPG sensation and more gems are leaving in October
items.content:
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 was one of 2025’s best games and one of the best third-party releases ever to join Game Pass day-and-date. Players have now had over a year to finish the turn-based RPG, but for any subscribers who haven’t yet taken the plunge, time is running out. The GOTY winner is leaving Game Pass on October 15.

That leaves you just under two weeks to go and complete the journey or start it from scratch. You can rush the main story to clear it in under 30 hours, but if you want to mine all of the expanded content, a completionist run will take you more than twice that. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is one of the rare JRPG-inspired games that’s managed to break through in the modern era to a broader audience, in part thanks to its novel dodge and parry mechanics which inject some fresh energy into the usual turn-based grind. It’s also worth making it all the way through to hit the twist ending .

But Clair Obscur is also not the only great game leaving Game Pass this month . The full list includes:

Pacific Drive and A Plague Tale Requiem are both excellent, especially for the spooky month. The former is a sci-fi survival crafting game about navigating a zone full of strange anomalies with a haunted station wagon. The latter is about surviving a late medieval Europe infested with disease carrying rats. Donut County , on the other hand, is a light hearted puzzle game you can finish in just a few hours that is still one of my favorite indie games of all time.

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is now available in Arabic!

items.content:
Expeditioners!

Following the huge demand from so many of you, we’ve been working super hard to be able to finally announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, is now available with Arabic text!

This brings the total number of supported languages to 20!

With the new Arabic language support, we had to consider additional changes to the game’s UI to ensure a smooth and enjoyable experience for Arabic-speaking players around the world.

Adding Arabic localization has been a true team effort over many months, from the incredible adaptation and localization work carried out by the linguists, to reworking the vast majority of the user interface for right-to-left reading, all the way through localization testing.

Every team involved brought passion and dedication to making this possible, and we couldn’t be more grateful for their work. We hope this update makes the story feel even more personal to our players.

Today’s update also includes some additional fixes and improvements. Read the full patch notes here!

Thank you all so much for your continued support! <3

Tomorrow comes.

~ The Expedition 33 Team

items.title: 1st Anniversary of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
items.summary: Expeditioners!! Today marks 1 year since we released Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. This past year has been an incredible journey and so we have a few things to share with you today. To celebrate the occasion, the team put together a special
items.content:
Expeditioners!! 

 

Today marks 1 year since we released Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. This past year has been an incredible journey and so we have a few things to share with you today. 

 

To celebrate the occasion, the team put together a special piece of artwork that we hope you will enjoy! 

8 Million Copies Sold

We're so thrilled, and honestly still quite overwhelmed, to announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 has officially reached 8 million copies sold!

Thank you so so much to every single person who has played, created art, shared, streamed, discussed, and supported this game!!

Game Update: New Haircuts + Patch Notes

We've pushed a fun little update live today: new haircuts are now available in-game, giving the expedition even more style to strut around in! 💅 

For the full list of changes, fixes, and improvements, you can read the patch notes here

Community Emotes

Our community is packed with phenomenally talented artists and we wanted to celebrate that today.  

We commissioned some of our amazing community creators to design official Expedition 33 emotes for you to use in your own channels! 

A massive thank you to IrunoArt, comickergirl (Sarah Leuver), and Bugyakis for their brilliant work on each of these!!

They're FREE to download and use here

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Devs Won't Pick a Canon Ending as They Work on a Sequel: 'It Is a Schrodinger's Ending'
items.summary: This is an article about one of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's writers saying that the developers will not "canonize" one ending over the other, even as they work on future games set in the same universe.
items.content:
If you've finished Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , you probably have some strong opinions about the game's multiple possible endings. I feel like saying anything more about that at the top of this article would be irresponsible, but this is a story about one of the game's writers saying that developer Sandfall Interactive is not going to "canonize" one ending over the other, even as they work on future games set in the same universe.

As such, from now on, I'm going to talk as if you have beaten the game and seen at least one of the two endings. Huge spoilers for the ending of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 below the video! Read on at your own risk.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 offers two possible endings no matter how you choose to play the game or how much side content you do. At the end of the game, you can choose to control Maelle or Verso in a single battle against the other, and winning it gets you the ending of whichever character you picked. Already tragic enough, neither of these endings are very satisfying ones. Verso's ending offers emotional catharsis for both characters admittedly, but at the expense of the lives of most of the rest of the cast you've come to love up to that point. Maelle's keeps everyone alive and kicking, but at the cost of multiple people's free will and, arguably, Maelle's own life and sanity. The choice is rough, but also very much in keeping with who Verso and Maelle have shown themselves to be in the game up to this point.

But that does beg the question: which of these endings in the "real" or canon ending? You could argue that it doesn't matter, and it's up to the player, but developer Sandfall Interactive has confirmed it's working on another game in the same universe. It seems likely that at some point the story of any future game they make could brush up against the consequences of one choice or the other. And if that happens, they'll have to pick which option is the truly "canon" version. Right? Right?

Wrong, says writer Jennifer Svedberg-Yen in an interview I conducted at DICE Summit last month. "We are not going to pick one," she told me. When I pushed, asking if they'd truly never choose, she replied: "Never say never, but there is no canon ending there. It is a Schrodinger's ending."

Expedition 33's two tragic endings were apparently settled on by the writers early in the development process, according to Svedberg-Yen. They knew they wanted Maelle and Verso to fight, she says, and neither of them really care much for "storybook" happy endings.

"I think that was almost like an unspoken agreement," she continued. "We never even considered really a true, happy ending. I think there was maybe a happier one possibly. You can see also in the way that the endings are edited, that one has a slightly more uplifting tone and one has a slightly darker tone. That was a choice that Guillaume made in terms of just having a little bit of shading there. But from my perspective, narratively, both are equally valid. Both are both good and bad. And it really just depends on whose perspective, whose good or whose happily-ever-after you are prioritizing."

I guess at least that means Verso's ending gets to continue being canon in my own, personal mental lore.

We spoke to Svedberg-Yen on a number of other subjects, including the wild, winding road she took to becoming a writer on Expedition 33, the emotional inspiration for each of the main characters, and the silly bets her colleagues lost because the game did so well . You can read our full interview with her right here.

Rebekah Valentine is a senior reporter for IGN. Got a story tip? Send it to rvalentine@ign.com.

items.content:
Introducing a special bundle featuring the award‑winning fantasy RPG “Metaphor: ReFantazio”, created by the team behind Persona 3-5, paired with “Clair Obscur: Expedition 33” - now available at 10% off!

Enjoy both titles and experience the worlds for yourself!

The Metaphor: ReFantazio × Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Bundle includes two games: “Metaphor: ReFantazio” and “Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.”

Message from Guillaume Broche & Katsura Hashino

"Metaphor: ReFantazio is a game that is really inspiring for us. It tells a beautiful story in a completely new world that is masterfully crafted. It deals with heavy themes but one that resonates strongly with me is the importance of imagination in all aspects of our lives. The cast is lovable and the turn-based battle system is one of the best I have played. The re-imagination of the traditional jobs system through Archetypes is fantastic and opens up so many playstyles that are fun to play around with. On top of that, the game has one of the most charismatic villains I've ever seen in an RPG. It is a great honor to be able to collaborate with Atlus on this bundle, as I have been a fan of their work since Shin Megami Tensei: Lucifer's Call (also known as Shin Megami Tensei III Nocturne for some players)." - Guillaume Broche

"I am Katsura Hashino from ATLUS, serving as the Creative Director for “Metaphor: ReFantazio.” I am very pleased to hear that a Steam bundle will be released with “Expedition 33,” a title that has received high praise around the world.

“Expedition 33” is a work that conveys a deep understanding of and sincere dedication to the JRPG genre, crafted with great care down to the finest details. As someone who also creates RPGs, I found it to be truly inspiring.

I am genuinely delighted to see Japanese-style RPGs being born and embraced, not only from Japanese-based studios like ours, but other places around the world through diverse creative approaches.

While the two titles differ in their worlds and overall direction, players may find a shared spirit in how we each approach and express the RPG genre. I hope that this bundle encourages players to experience both titles and enjoy the breadth of what RPGs can offer."

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 | Dev Blog - Photo Mode
items.summary: Expeditioners, We're so pleased to see so many of you enjoying the new photo mode feature!! We put a lot of time and care into building this feature and we’re so glad to see so many of you enjoying it! There were a lot of moving parts invol
items.content:
Expeditioners,

We're so pleased to see so many of you enjoying the new photo mode feature!!

We put a lot of time and care into building this feature and we’re so glad to see so many of you enjoying it! There were a lot of moving parts involved in getting the Photo Mode set up, so we thought we’d show a bit of the process in this blog and talk a bit about what went into building this feature.

There were a few key people involved in the development of this, and each of them had a part to write here !

VINCENT CONSTANTIN-TURKI – Producer \

One of the main features we wanted to introduce with the Thank You Update was Photo Mode. It felt like a meaningful way to give something back to the players and thank them for their commitment to the game.

What’s funny is that the team in charge of developing Photo Mode doesn’t usually use this feature in other games, which is why we decided to collaborate with Shinobi. He helped us design a Photo Mode that would truly resonate with players.

NAJA DALMAGNE – QA Coordinator \

In many games we tested, Photo Modes often felt restrictive, which could quickly become frustrating. So, from the very beginning, one of the key goals we all agreed on was to give players as much freedom as possible. It was really about letting players express their creativity without getting in the way.

During development, the QA team ran into some unexpected and sometimes quite funny issues. One of the funniest, but also one of the most severe, involved characters whose heads or torsos could become displaced or deformed when opening the Photo Mode if they hadn’t been visible on screen for a while during exploration.

One feature I’m particularly proud of is the lighting system Florian worked on. It offers great flexibility while remaining fairly easy to use, which really makes a difference when you're trying to get the perfect shot.

FLORIAN TORRES – Senior Gameplay Programmer \ \

I love giving players as many tools and features as possible (that’s literally the purpose of my job).

When we started working on the photo mode, our goal was to give players as few restrictions as possible and that’s what I was in charge of coding: infinite camera distance, the ability to pass through collisions, lots of customizable lights, many (weird) filters, and more.

Of course, that comes with its challenges, but in the end it allows players to see a lot of things we don’t want to show during normal gameplay. The photo mode became a way to peek behind the scenes of each cinematic or environment, and sometimes even see how we have created the entire game.

Ever wondered what happens outside the camera frame? Here’s an example (sorry cinematic team, I love you).

LUDOVIC ‘SHINOBI’ HELME – Photo Mode Consultant \

We felt it was important to include anything that increases the “freedom” factor for players. It opens up countless possibilities every time someone enters photo mode: a very generous camera range to capture unseen details or create epic compositions, RGB curves control to edit and build your own color schemes, a strong custom lighting system to truly take ownership of a scene, and solid depth-of-field management.

But when all of that is also available in cutscenes - giving access to those incredible facial expressions and emotions - that’s when I really start to feel satisfied.

Every shot I’ve seen has blown my mind, and I often wish I’d been the one to come up with the idea. It’s truly inspiring.

I’m very proud that the team managed to create a tool that is both beginner-friendly and deeply satisfying for more experienced photographers. Finding that balance is extremely difficult.

With all of these features, there had to be a user-friendly way for people to make use of everything. Making sure players had full control of all the settings and could navigate all the features comes down to our awesome Gameplay & UI Programmer, VICTOR BOULEZ.

Thank you for all of your appreciation and feedback on this feature, we had a lot of fun making it and even more fun watching you use it!

This past week, especially, we’ve really loved the work you’ve all been putting into the social Photo Mode Prompt Challenge!! We’ve seen some amazing photography this past week, it’s completely blown our minds how creative you have been able to get with the prompts and tools.

Even though the challenge is over, feel free to keep sharing your work with us on social media, we thoroughly enjoy seeing some of your masterpieces!!

In the meantime, we are continuing to work on fixes for ongoing problems, keep an eye on the bug thread and socials to stay updated on the latest.

Finally, we leave you with some of our favourite uses of photo mode.

items.title: I played Cory in the House for Nintendo DS to find out if it’s truly better than Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
items.summary: I played the Disney game threatening Clair Obscur: Expedition 33’s top Metacritic ranking — is it actually good?
items.content:
When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works .

(Image credit: Future / Nintendo / Disney / Sandfall Interactive / Kepler Interactive) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Threads Email Share this article 9 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Cory in the House for the Nintendo DS. That’s a name I haven’t heard in a long time. See, this 2008-released ‘adventure stealth’ game – as well as the TV show it’s based on – has been a meme for more than a decade. In the past, I’d often see Cory in the House being described as the ‘best anime of all time’. I’d also read Amazon reviews of the video game, which would hail it as a true ‘masterpiece’.

And now, in 2026, the meme seems to have been reborn. Users have taken to Metacritic and flooded it with positive reviews for Cory in the House on the Nintendo DS. And now, its user score sits at 9.3, which is indicative of ‘universal acclaim’. That score is so high, in fact, that the title is genuinely posing a threat to the top-ranked game on Metacritic by user score. And that game is none other than TechRadar’s Game of the Year of 2025, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 .

After hearing all of this, you may be wondering: is Cory in the House on Nintendo DS actually good? Well, it’s your lucky day. See, back in my teens, a friend of mine jokingly gifted me the game for Christmas, and thankfully, I still own it to this day. So, I dusted the cartridge off, put it in my Nintendo 3DS console, and played through it for the very first time. Here’s what I made of my time with the ‘universally acclaimed’ title.

My game card didn’t work at first, but after a few blows and re-insertions, I was finally in. When I reached the main menu, there were a few options to choose from, including Story, an arcade mode, and a gallery. I got straight into the Story mode, and well…it was quite something.

In this campaign, you play as Cory Baxter, a teenager whose dad works as the head chef at The White House. As an aspiring businessman, Cory decides to sell bobbleheads of the President to the people of Washington DC – but trouble is afoot. See, an evil toymaker has turned the bobbleheads into hypnotic devices, and it’s your job to foil their malign scheme. Ridiculous? Absolutely. But I came into this experience with an open heart and an open mind.

I wasn't convinced by Elden Ring Tarnished Edition until I played it on Nintendo Switch 2 After parting ways with Xbox, I pray that Double Fine is working on more games like Psychonauts 2 — one of the best platformers since Super Mario Odyssey Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave review: the best game on Nintendo Switch 2 so far However, as soon as I got into the game, I was instantly struck by frankly horrifying visuals. No, really, I have a feeling Cory’s face will be haunting my nightmares for the foreseeable future. See, characters are so unrefined and blurred that you can’t even see their eyes or expressions. And that’s not inherent to the console – plenty of DS games pulled off nice-looking character models in spite of the handheld’s technical limitations.

Anyway, that’s not the end of the world, at least the gameplay could still be fun! Right? Well, I suppose in a sense, Cory in the House truly is a genre-defining title; in that it defines exactly how not to make an adventure stealth game. Movement is janky, throwing exploding fictional pastries is, somehow, totally mind-numbing, and the various settings are unbelievably bland. You play the occasional mini-game to progress the story, but even these are so laughably basic that I can’t even imagine a child having fun.

Oh, and one more thing. You have a lot of conversations with characters like Cory’s father, bandmates, and store workers – many of which are intended to be funny…at least I think they are? Sometimes I was unsure whether Cory was trying to crack a joke, but luckily, a laugh track would play when it was time for me to giggle. Artificial laughs even seem to play when characters don’t say anything remotely funny, which in itself was actually kinda entertaining. So, I guess there’s that?

So, there you have it, folks. Cory in the House for the Nintendo DS is – in spite of its 9.3 user score on Metacritic – a pretty terrible TV show tie-in, and it’s no wonder that its two critic review scores are listed as a 30 and a 40. Ouch.

Still, I’ve been finding the explosion of ironic meme-fuelled positive reviews pretty funny, even as a massive lover of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . And while we’re here, it only seems right to recommend this actual masterpiece to anyone who hasn’t tried it yet.

Resident Evil 2 for Nintendo Switch 2 review: survival horror mastery on the go Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse review: a classic platformer given fresh new blood Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter review: yet another triumphant remake Yes, Expedition 33 is a phenomenal RPG, with one of the best stories that’s ever been told through the video game medium, in my view. It plates up incredibly addictive gameplay, with an excellent parrying mechanic that’s a joy to master. Combine that with a jaw-droppingly gorgeous visual style and generational soundtrack, and it’s simply a must-play.

No matter how good it is, though, it may not be able to stop the immovable force that is Cory in the House for the Nintendo DS, which, in its own ‘special’ way, is a game that I won’t be forgetting in a hurry.

items.title: How ‘Clair Obscur: Expedition 33’ Revitalized the RPG and Won Game of the Year
items.summary: A French turn-based RPG made for under $10 million somehow managed to be the defining game of 2025. Now, Hollywood is calling.
items.content:
This year, gamers beheld the strangest of success stories: (1) A French video game publisher (2) that isn’t Ubisoft (3) partnered with a rookie studio (4) that is also French (5) to release a turn-based role-playing game (6) with a decidedly Parisian flamboyance (7) that would commercially outperform every other single-player title out this year by a mile.

The game was Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . Its developer, Sandfall Interactive, and its publisher, Kepler Interactive, were hardly household names upon the game’s release in April 2025; both companies were founded in just the past couple of years, during COVID, and while Kepler already had one hit to its credit in Sifu , Clair Obscur was, in fact, the debut title for Sandfall Interactive. This was a less than $10 million project in a world of $200 million franchise titles. Yet Clair Obscur was a blockbuster in scope and a marvel in several aspects of its execution—in its wonderfully tense combat, in its immense musical score, in its gorgeous art direction, in its remarkably mature writing. It was shockingly on par with Final Fantasy . It was, in fact, something bigger.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 sold 1 million copies in three days and more than 6 million copies by the end of the year. It’s become the year’s defining video game release, and it’s slated to become a full franchise, from a studio that is only getting started. The Hollywood production company Story Kitchen, which specializes in video game adaptations, is already handling a live-action film adaptation of Clair Obscur . Earlier this month, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, publicly congratulated Sandfall after Clair Obscur swept the Game Awards in Los Angeles, beating Death Stranding 2 and Hollow Knight: Silksong for Game of the Year.

Beginning in the dreamy island town of Lumière—conspicuously evocative of Paris circa the Belle Époque— Clair Obscur is the story of a defiant humanity staring down the threat of extinction.

Lumière is haunted by a distant figure known as the Paintress, who oversees an ominous countdown that’s displayed on the face of a monolith that looms over the horizon. The countdown drops by one each year, and the number represents an age: Anyone at or over the age that’s currently displayed is erased from existence, in an annual phenomenon known as the gommage. These heartless erasures leave the survivors ever more desperate to vanquish the Paintress. The beleaguered people of Lumière send waves of armed expeditions to the monolith across the sea. The dozens of expeditions to date have all failed, littering the landscape with withered corpses, ruined campsites, and scattered logs of each team’s discoveries in the treacherous world beyond Lumière.

A young soldier named Gustave leads Expedition 33, the latest, fateful voyage to defeat the Paintress. So we follow Gustave, Maelle, Lune, Sciel, and a few other stragglers through a series of uncomfortable subversions of the genre’s standard sentimental journey to save the world. In so many ways, Clair Obscur ends in a place very different from where it began, after a series of profound revelations and existential reckonings straight from Sartre and Descartes. The game’s director, Guillaume Broche, thus pitched Clair Obscur to its composer, Lorien Testard: “You arrive at the beginning of the game after the heroes have already lost.”

Chiefly, Clair Obscur tends to draw comparisons to Final Fantasy X , a game that’s similarly concerned with a world-saving pilgrimage that was secretly doomed from the very start. The comparison is still more striking at the historical level: FFX is widely seen as both the technical and commercial peak of the triple-A turn-based RPG, preceding a couple of decades of agonizing among some players about the inventiveness and the fashionability of these sorts of games.

RPG Party: ‘Clair Obscur: Expedition 33’ and ‘The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Remastered’

svg]:ui-size-4 p-0 ui-bg-transparent ui-text-brand-orange ui-flex md:ui-hidden" data-sentry-component="MediumIcon" data-sentry-source-file="index.tsx"> Button Mash Button Mash On the one hand, games like Persona 5 , Octopath Traveler , Metaphor: ReFantazio , and now Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 are some of the bestselling single-player titles of the past decade, and they’re all turn-based RPGs. Still, the heyday of the turn-based RPG was squarely in the late ’90s through the early 2000s, with their popularity having since waned in favor of real-time, action-based RPGs such as Elden Ring . Square Enix, the longtime publisher of Final Fantasy , has for the past several years struggled to adapt its banner franchise to these shifting sensibilities; Final Fantasy XV and the most recent Final Fantasy XVI both implemented purely action-based combat systems, to the widespread displeasure of many longtime fans of the series. (The ongoing remake trilogy for Final Fantasy VII , a turn-based classic, uses a peculiar hybrid system for its combat: free, real-time movement with turn-based actions.)

Sandfall opted to integrate real-time prompts into the turn-based combat of Clair Obscur . Here, the player selects a move for a character in battle—a basic attack, a healing spell, a party buff, etc.—and then executes quick time inputs during the move’s animation in order to increase its effectiveness. More importantly, Clair Obscur lets players respond to incoming attacks by dodging, parrying, or jumping, depending on the type of attack. These defensive options, varying in execution difficulty, give the player opportunities to avoid taking any damage from a hit, with a successful parry of an entire combo also unleashing an instant counterattack. So here we have a system of turn-based combat that tests a player’s real-time reflexes, akin to a rhythm game, rewarding a mix of savviness in weapon selection, stat management, and party composition, as in classic turn-based RPGs.

Clair Obscur feels like a distinct breakthrough, though not for a lack of creative effort by the industry in previous years to reinvent the turn-based RPG. The cult classic Lost Odyssey , for instance, experimented with timed, reflex-based elements in turn-based combat to divisive effect in the era of its release. This is the typical conundrum for developers hoping to reinvigorate or revolutionize the turn-based RPG: how to improve upon the old mechanics rather than distort them in the hands of their most loyal fan bases. Broche has cited Lost Odyssey as a major influence in the development of Clair Obscur . He approached his game’s release date with a certain mischievous daring, a willingness to treat experimental features as unquestionably ready—no, destined—for prime time.
